planting.note: Pot in a fine-bark or bark-and-sphagnum terrestrial mix in bright shade; this is the plant that started Paphiopedilum breeding, so it tolerates typical mottled-leaf slipper culture with average home warmth.

directions: Raised by Veitch nursery in 1869 from Paphiopedilum villosum crossed with P. barbatum, this cross is generally regarded as the first Paphiopedilum hybrid ever bloomed. The clump-forming, strap-shaped leaves are plain deep green, and a single rounded flower in warm coppery-brown and maroon tones appears on a short stem in winter. It remains in cultivation today as a vigorous, easy grower, prized more for its place in orchid history than for novelty of color. Keep the mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, since Paphiopedilum has no water-storing pseudobulbs.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Grow in a small pot of fine bark or bark-sphagnum mix in bright shade; a cool-tolerant, easy-blooming slipper orchid suited to a windowsill or unheated greenhouse bench.

directions: Registered in 1884 from a cross of Paphiopedilum insigne and P. spicerianum, this was among the earliest successful hybrids to exploit the vigor and free-flowering habit of P. insigne, a quality that made insigne a favorite parent throughout the Victorian orchid-hybridizing boom. The rounded, domed dorsal sepal shows the pale ground and dark veining inherited from spicerianum, set above yellow-green petals flushed with mahogany. Flowering in winter, a single bloom can last two months or more on a well-grown plant. It grows readily in average home conditions and needs less warmth than tropical Paphiopedilum species.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark in bright, filtered light; a vigorous fall-blooming classic still widely grown more than a century after its introduction.

directions: Bred by Veitch nursery in 1897 by crossing the clustering, cane-forming Guarianthe bowringiana with the large-flowered Cattleya labiata, this was one of the first hybrids to combine the two distinct growth lines within the Cattleya alliance. The result is a tall, floriferous plant carrying full heads of soft rose-lavender flowers accented by a deep magenta lip with a golden throat, blooming reliably in autumn. Over a century of continuous cultivation and repeated re-awarding of exceptional clones attest to its lasting garden and greenhouse value. Grow it like a standard Cattleya, with bright light, a distinct wet-dry watering cycle, and a period of slightly cooler, drier rest after flowering.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Pot in coarse bark in bright, filtered light; unusually among Cattleyas this hybrid does not stick to a single bloom season, so plants can flush at various times of year.

directions: Introduced by Veitch nursery in 1898 from a cross of Cattleya mossiae and C. warscewiczii, Enid combines the free-flowering habit of mossiae with the large size and rich color of warscewiczii. Flowers are light rose-purple with a deeply ruffled, crimson-purple lip opening into a bright yellow throat, and unlike many Cattleyas the hybrid is not confined to its parents' natural bloom windows, flowering somewhat unpredictably across the year. It has remained a benchmark cross for over a century, with numerous awarded clones bred from carefully selected parent plants. Give it bright light, a coarse free-draining bark mix, and a brief drier rest between root flushes.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

planting.note: Give it a large pot of coarse bark mix and a cool autumn night drop to trigger spiking; this standard-type cymbidium is the ancestor behind an enormous share of modern large-flowered hybrids.

directions: Raised by Sir George Holford in 1911 from Cymbidium eburneo-lowianum crossed with C. insigne, this grex became historically pivotal when its 'Westonbirt' clone, first exhibited in 1922, proved to be a spontaneous tetraploid with four sets of chromosomes rather than the usual two. That chromosome doubling made 'Westonbirt' an exceptionally potent breeding parent, and a large share of the large-flowered cymbidium hybrids grown commercially today trace back to it. Flowers are broad and waxy, pale cream to white with rose-red markings on the lip, carried in arching sprays through winter and early spring. Grow in bright, filtered light with a distinct cool snap in autumn to set spikes, and expect it to bloom best when slightly pot-bound.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register

common_name: Doris Phalaenopsis (Foundational White Moth Orchid Grex)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant in coarse bark media with excellent drainage; a historically important white-flowered grex that sits behind much of the modern potted Phalaenopsis trade.

directions: Registered by Duke Farms in 1940 from Phalaenopsis Elisabethae crossed with Phal. Katherine Siegwart, both themselves complex descendants of P. amabilis, this grex became one of the most influential white-flowered Phalaenopsis lines of the twentieth century, producing a string of individually awarded clones over the following decades. Its broad, flat, pure white flowers with a touch of yellow and red in the lip established a benchmark form that later breeders used repeatedly in developing the large, round-flowered white Phalaenopsis hybrids common in the trade today. Plants form a modest fan of thick, glossy leaves and send up arching spikes carrying multiple long-lasting blooms. Grow in bright indirect light and coarse bark, allowing the mix to dry slightly between waterings.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society International Orchid Register
